power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

Publicly available equations, reference curves, and standardized Z-scores could improve individualized interpretation and comparability across biomarkers, laboratories, and clinical populations.
Blood biomarkers are increasingly used to support the diagnosis and monitoring of neurodegenerative diseases.

However, their interpretation is complicated by physiological determinants, including age, sex, body-mass index, and renal function, and by differences in absolute concentrations between analytical methods.
We aimed to develop population-based reference equations allowing individualized interpretation of selected blood biomarkers blood biomarkers used in neurology.
In this cross-sectional study, we analysed plasma samples from cognitively unimpaired participants selected from the French CONSTANCES and Three-City population-based cohorts.

Generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape were used to model neurofilament light chain (NfL), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), phosphorylated tau 181 (p-tau181), amyloid-β40, amyloid-β42, and their ratios according to age, sex, body-mass index, and renal function.
The resulting equations provided individualized expected concentrations, percentiles, and Z-scores.
Previously established disease-specific concentrations were converted into Z-score.
Cross-calibration equations were developed for NfL measurements across analytical methods and sample matrices.
The final reference populations comprised 5123 participants for amyloid biomarkers and p-tau181 and 5122 for NfL and GFAP; median age was 52.3 years and 49.7% were women.
Between ages 40 and 80 years, expected NfL and GFAP concentrations increased by an average of 2.6% and 2.2% per year, respectively.
Renal function, body-mass index, and sex had additional biomarker-specific effects.

text.text: Among biological fluids, blood is the most widely used and accessible medium for biological analysis, carrying a broad range of circulating proteins that reflect systemic physiological and pathological processes.

In neurodegenerative and neuroinflammatory diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), metabolites and proteins associated with pathological processes in the central nervous system (CNS) can cross the blood-brain barrier and reach the bloodstream, allowing their use as blood-based biomarkers.

The detection of CNS-derived biomarkers in blood has historically been challenging because their concentrations are substantially lower than those observed in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), mainly due to dilution.
The emergence of ultrasensitive approaches, such as SIMOA (2), has opened new avenues for the detection of CNS biomarkers in the blood.

After an initial phase of validation, the demonstration that blood-based biomarkers could match the clinical performance of CSF biomarkers initiated a major transformation in the diagnosis of neurological diseases and was accompanied by new assays on clinical routine analyzers, whose sensitivity has been improved.

For example, the biological diagnosis of AD, which relies on the detection of pathologically relevant amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptides and phosphorylated tau (p-tau) proteins in the CSF, is rapidly shifting toward blood-based biomarkers (3) (4) (5) (6).

text.text: Detection of the astrocytic glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), as a marker of astrocytic activation and damage, is moving to the blood (7) (8) (9).

text.text: Importantly, plasma GFAP has shown stronger associations with ADrelated amyloid pathology than CSF GFAP (10), whereas CSF GFAP has demonstrated limited diagnostic performance across dementia syndromes (11).

text.text: Neurofilament light chain protein (NfL), which is released upon axonal damage of various origins, is another example of a blood-based biomarker (12, 13), with in vitro diagnostic (IVD)-certified methods now available in routine lab settings.

text.text: Thus, we observed an exponential and rapid development in the use of these biomarkers for the biological diagnosis of neurological diseases.
The interpretation of blood-based biomarkers remains complex (12), as their values are affected by several physiological factors, such as age, sex, body mass index (BMI) and renal function (14).

text.text: Thus, covariate-adjusted reference values are needed to guide interpretation, and to distinguish normal from abnormal changes.
Several studies have developed these reference values, mostly for NfL and GFAP.
For NfL, age has been consistently associated with higher concentrations (9, (15) (16) (17) (18) (19) (20), while other studies also reported an inverse association with BMI (9, 20).

text.text: Renal function may represent another important determinant, with lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) associated with higher NfL concentrations reported (9).

text.text: Importantly, most available reference data for NfL and GFAP were generated using Simoa-based assays, which may limit their applicability across analytical platforms.
In addition, reference values for other biomarkers are still limited, notably for AD-related biomarkers, including Aβ and p-tau.
Indeed, their interpretation are now well-established in a pathological context.
For example, in AD and related pathologies, Aβ42 and the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio generally decrease, whereas p-tau tend to increase (18).

text.text: However, among cognitively healthy participants without underlying pathologies, the change of these biomarkers is yet to be characterized.

Cooper et al. reported that, among Canadian participants aged 3-79 years, the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio showed a slight decrease with age, whereas p-tau181 followed a Ushaped association, with concentrations decreasing during childhood and increasing in later adulthood cooper (16).

text.text: Accounting for other physiological determinants is needed for these biomarkers, as previous studies have shown that plasma levels of Aβ proteins and p-tau tend to increase with impaired renal function and decrease at higher levels of BMI (21, 22).

text.text: In this study, we developed reference values for a selection of relevant blood biomarkers of neurodegenerative diseases, including Aβ and p-tau proteins, NFL and GFAP using a large population-based cohort, measured with Roche Elecsys assay.
We accounted for the effects of age, sex, BMI, and renal function, which are known to influence blood biomarker concentrations to varying degrees depending on the analyte (23).
text.formatted: We accounted for the effects of age, sex, BMI, and renal function, which are known to influence blood biomarker concentrations to varying degrees depending on the analyte <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(23)</ref>.

text.text: We also determined the optimal thresholds for normalized biomarkers using different IVD assays to detect AD, ALS, and MS.
And finally, we provided cross-calibration equations to facilitate harmonization across different analytical platforms and biological fluids.

The final goal is to provide the community with accessible equations and reference plots for direct clinical use, thereby improving the quality, interpretation, and performance of blood-based biomarkers for patient management in neurodegenerative and neurological disorders.

text.text: Relative covariate-related percentage changes were estimated using the fitted median (Z-score=0) biomarker values for women relative to men for each additional 1 year between 40 and 80 years, each unit increase in BMI between 20 and 40 kg/m², and 5 units increase in creatinine between 50 and 120 µmol/L. The 40-80-year interval was selected to provide a standardized summary of age-related changes across biomarkers.
As age effects may be nonlinear, these average annual changes should not be interpreted as constant rates across the full age range covered by the reference curves.
Population-based reference distributions were estimated using inverse probability weighted (IPW) generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS) (34).
text.formatted: Population-based reference distributions were estimated using inverse probability weighted (IPW) generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(34)</ref>.

text.text: These models allow the location, dispersion, skewness, and kurtosis of biomarker distributions to vary according to individual characteristics and are therefore well-suited for the derivation of age-and covariate-specific reference values.
Inverse probability weights were used to account for the sampling design and non-response.
CONSTANCES participants received three weights (sampling cohort, sampling substudy, and nonresponse), whereas 3C participants received a rescaled weight based on national demographic distributions.
The final weights were computed by multiplying the components.

Four distributions: Box-Cox Cole Green (BCCG), Box-Cox T (BCT), Box-Cox power exponential (BCPE) and normal distributions were tested, with BCT providing the lowest Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) for all the biomarkers.
BCT includes four distribution parameters: median µ, scale parameter σ (approximation of the coefficient of variation), skewness v, and kurtosis τ.
Creatinine and eGFR were compared as alternative markers of renal function using the AIC.
Creatinine-based models provided a better fit for all biomarkers except the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio and were therefore retained in the final models to ensure consistency across biomarkers.
Two sets of candidate covariates were considered for each biomarker: Model 1 included age, sex, BMI, and creatinine, whereas Model 2 considered only age and sex.
Within each model, covariates were retained according to their contribution to model fit, as determined by the predefined selection procedure.
For µ, covariates were added incrementally to the model and retained if they significantly reduced the AIC.
Additionally, cohort effects were tested.
For the selected continuous variables, linear and fractional polynomial terms (degrees 1 or 2) were tested.
The same selection procedure for variables as for µ was applied for σ and v.
To avoid overfitting, τ was not regressed on the covariates.

The estimated distribution parameters (μ, σ, ν, and τ) were used to calculate the adjusted percentiles and Z-scores through a four-step procedure, allowing the interpretation of an individual concentration relative to the expected distribution in the reference population.

Finally, age-specific reference curves were generated from the fitted models and plotted for selected Z-scores (0, 1, 1.5, and 2), stratified by creatinine concentrations (50, 80, and 100 µmol/L), BMI levels (20, 25, and 30 kg/m²), and sex.

These values were selected for illustrative purposes: BMI values of 25 and 30 kg/m² correspond to the conventional thresholds for overweight and obesity, respectively, whereas creatinine concentrations of 50, 80, and 100 µmol/L represent different physiological profiles rather than established clinical cut-offs.
To evaluate the impact of physiological adjustment, we compared unadjusted Z-scores with Z-scores adjusted for age and sex (Model 2) and those additionally adjusted for BMI and creatinine (Model 1)..
Linear regression models were then used to investigate the associations between diagnostic group and Z-score values for each approach.

Disease-specific thresholds previously established in independent studies performed on the same analytical platforms were converted into Z-score thresholds using the reference equations developed in the present study.
Deming regression was performed to derive cross-calibration equations that allowed conversion between analytical platforms (35).

Using these cross-calibration equations, the Z-score values were transformed to the Lumipulse IVD assay scale.

Age-specific reference curves were then generated from the fitted models and plotted for selected Z-scores (0, 1, 1.5, and 2), stratified by creatinine concentrations (50, 80, and 100 µmol/L) for NfL levels.
In addition, equations were used to calculate the Z-scores in the clinical cohorts.
Linear regression models were fitted to assess the association between diagnosis and Z-scores.
Finally, threshold values for the relevant biomarkers were estimated for each diagnosis by maximizing the Youden index.

text.text: Overall, disease-associated differences were largely preserved across the three approaches, although physiological adjustment modified their magnitude without consistently increasing disease-control separation.

For GFAP, the highest values were observed in AD participants compared to controls (β = 1.28, 95% CI 0.89-1.67 with the model 1), while PPMS and FTD exhibited more moderate elevations of GFAP Z-scores.
In contrast, p-tau181 Z-scores were selectively increased in AD (β = 1.95, 95% CI 1.59-2.32 with the model 1).

For NfL, Z-scores values were consistently elevated across all diagnostic groups except RRMS, with the largest increases observed in FTD (β = 1.61, 95% CI: 1.06-2.17 with the model 1), consistent with widespread neuroaxonal injury.

The magnitude of the estimated differences was generally slightly reduced within the adjusted models, although the overall pattern of biomarker alterations across diagnostic groups remained largely consistent across the three models.

text.text: In this study, we established population-based reference values for five individual blood biomarkers of neurodegenerative diseases, including NfL, GFAP, Aβ40, Aβ42, p-tau181, and two biomarker ratios, Aβ42/Aβ40 and p-tau181/Aβ42.

Using a large reference population comprising more than 5,000 cognitively unimpaired individuals' representative of the French population, we developed percentiles and Z-scores adjusted for major physiological determinants.

To facilitate implementation in clinical and research settings, we provide both mathematical equations and graphical reference curves, allowing the direct conversion of biomarker concentrations into standardized scores.
Their clinical relevance has been illustrated in independent cohorts, including AD, FTD, ALS, and MS.

Importantly, although physiological adjustment modifies disease-control differences, this does not necessarily translate into improved diagnostic accuracy, which was not directly assessed in this comparison.
Population-based reference studies have increasingly extended beyond NfL.

text.text: Direct numerical comparisons of reference limits across studies remain challenging because of differences in analytical platforms, sample matrices, population characteristics, and covariate adjustment strategies.
Our study complements these investigations by providing covariate-adjusted reference equations and individualized Zscores for five blood biomarkers and two ratios measured using Roche Elecsys assays.

The covariate effects observed in our study were consistent with those reported in previous studies of biomarker reference values, which showed that NfL (9, 15-20), GFAP (9, 15, 16), p-tau181 (16) levels increased with age and with impaired levels of renal function marker and lower BMI.

In addition, the annual percentage changes estimated in our study were within the range previously reported in the literature, with increases of approximately 3-4% per year for NfL (16, 19), 2% for GFAP (16), and approximately 3% for p-tau181 among individuals aged 60 years and older (16).

text.text: We also observed consistently higher levels of these biomarkers among women compared with men.
Our findings are consistent with those reported by Rousset et al. for GFAP, although other studies have not observed a significant association between sex and GFAP levels.
This discrepancy may be attributable to differences in study populations, age distributions, analytical platforms, or other unmeasured biological or methodological factors.
Physiological factors influence circulating biomarker concentrations to markedly different extents.
NfL and GFAP, which are non-specific biomarkers to neurodegenerative disease, are the most influenced by age, while creatinine has strong influence on NfL and p-tau181.
The inverse associations with BMI may partly reflect a blood-volume dilution effect, as previously proposed for NfL (14).

text.text: The association with age remained significant, even after adjusting for renal function.

However, renal function was assessed using creatinine, which is an imperfect surrogate of kidney function, particularly in older individuals, where creatinine levels are strongly influenced by muscle mass (40).

text.text: Recent studies have highlighted the important influence of kidney function on blood-based neurological biomarkers (23), and our study confirmed and quantified this effect.

text.text: However, the influence of renal function on biomarker concentrations does not necessarily translate into improved diagnostic accuracy after adjustment.

Arslan et al. (41) reported that adding eGFR to models including plasma biomarkers, age, and sex did not improve amyloid-positivity discrimination, although their cohort predominantly included individuals with preserved or mildly impaired renal function.

text.text: Sex-related differences were also observed across most biomarkers, with women generally exhibiting higher expected concentrations than men after adjusting for other covariates, particularly for GFAP, NfL, and p-tau181.

Previous population-based reference studies have reported inconsistent sex effects ranging from no detectable differences across biomarkers (16), to higher GFAP concentrations in women (9), suggesting that these associations may depend on the population studied and the biomarker considered.
The biological basis for this difference remains incompletely understood.
The persistence of a sex effect after adjustment for BMI and renal function suggests that sex captures additional biological determinants that are not fully explained by these variables.

Population-specific differences in cumulative behavioural and health-related exposures may also contribute to the heterogeneity observed across studies.Consequently, sex appears to be an important component of individualized biomarker interpretations.
The influence of age, renal function, BMI, and sex was not uniform across all biomarkers.
Aβ peptides, which have both central and peripheral origins, were less influenced by BMI.
Notably, Aβ42/Aβ40 and p-tau181/Aβ42 were less strongly influenced by these physiological determinants.

This likely reflects the fact that both analytes composing the ratio are influenced in similar ways by these physiological factors, such that calculating the ratio tends to offset their effects (42) (43) (44).

text.text: The establishment of normative equations made it possible to express biomarker concentrations as standardized Z-scores rather than relying solely on absolute concentrations.
Standardized Z-scores reduce physiological variability attributable to age, sex, BMI, and renal function, thereby improving the comparability across individuals.

In addition, because all biomarkers are expressed in standard deviation units, Z-scores enable direct comparison of abnormalities across biomarkers, despite their different analytical scales and concentration ranges.

Similar to pediatric growth charts or bone mineral density Z-scores, this framework expresses biomarker concentrations relative to the expected distribution for an individual with similar physiological characteristics.
Z-scores also facilitate longitudinal monitoring by enabling changes to be interpreted relative to the expected biological variation.
This normalization may improve diagnostic and prognostic assessments by distinguishing diseaserelated biomarker abnormalities from physiological variations.
Individualized reference equations may be useful in several clinical settings.
First, they may facilitate the interpretation of biomarker results in routine laboratory practice by providing standardized measures of abnormalities.
Second, they may improve harmonization across clinical centers by reducing the variability attributable to differences in patient characteristics.
Third, they may support patient selection, risk stratification, and treatment monitoring in the clinical trials.
This approach may be especially valuable in older populations, where physiological increases in biomarker concentrations complicate the interpretation of the absolute values.
The potential clinical benefit of these reference equations is likely biomarkerdependent.

For NfL and GFAP, which are relatively nonspecific and strongly influenced by physiological factors, adjusted Z-scores may help identify elevations beyond those expected for an individual's physiological profile.

In contrast, for AD-related biomarkers such as p-tau181, disease-associated changes may substantially exceed physiological variability, and established assay-specific diagnostic cut-offs validated against amyloid PET or CSF biomarkers should remain the primary basis for diagnostic classification.
Adjusted Z-scores may provide complementary information, particularly for borderline values or patients with relevant comorbidities, but their additional diagnostic value remains to be established.
Such individualized interpretation aligns with the broader movement toward precision medicine and may facilitate the integration of blood biomarkers into routine neurological care in the future.
Disease-associated biomarker profiles remained largely consistent after adjustment for physiological covariates, without clear evidence of improved diagnostic discrimination.
Nevertheless, adjusted Z-scores provide a standardized measure of biomarker deviations relative to the expected distribution for individuals with comparable physiological characteristics.
Benkert et al. (20) demonstrated that age-and BMI-adjusted serum NfL Zscores improved the identification of disease activity and prognostication in MS compared with absolute concentration cutoffs.
text.formatted: Benkert et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(20)</ref> demonstrated that age-and BMI-adjusted serum NfL Zscores improved the identification of disease activity and prognostication in MS compared with absolute concentration cutoffs.

text.text: In our study, we found that accounting for creatinine and BMI may slightly attenuate NfL association with MS clinical phenotypes, underlying that part of the differences may be due to underlying comorbidities.
However, overall patterns are consistent.

Rather than masking disease-related biological differences, Z-scores enable biomarker abnormalities to be interpreted relative to the expected value for an individual with a similar age, sex, BMI, and renal function.
However, physiological normalization does not confer disease specificity.

Even biomarkers considered relatively specific for AD, such as p-tau181 and p-tau217, may be elevated in other neurological disorders, including Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (45) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (46) .

text.text: As blood biomarkers are generally measured in patients with a clinical suspicion of neurological disease, Z-scores should be interpreted in the context of the clinical presentation and complementary diagnostic investigations, rather than considered as standalone evidence of AD.
In addition to individualized interpretation, this study also provides assay conversion equations between major analytical platforms, including Elecsys®, Lumipulse®, Ella®, and Simoa® assays.
Although blood biomarkers are increasingly used in both research and clinical settings, substantial inter-method variability remains a major obstacle to their implementation.
Absolute concentrations may differ considerably between assays, despite excellent correlations.

Combined with assay conversion equations, expressing biomarker concentrations as percentiles or Z-scores relative to a common reference population provides a unified interpretative framework across the analytical platforms.
Such harmonization could facilitate the comparison of results between studies, laboratories, and healthcare systems.
Standardized reference values may contribute to future international efforts aimed at biomarker standardization and regulatory implementation.
This study had several important strengths.
First, it is based on a large reference population exceeding 5,000 participants, making it one of the largest normative studies of blood neurodegeneration biomarkers to date.
Another strength of this study is the simultaneous evaluation of several clinically relevant biomarkers using a unified statistical framework.

Finally, the use of GAMLSS modeling allowed us to estimate not only the mean biomarker values but also the age-dependent changes in variability, skewness, and kurtosis, providing a more flexible representation of biomarker distributions than conventional linear approaches.
This study has several limitations.
First, the study population was predominantly composed of French individuals of European ancestry, and external validation in more diverse populations is necessary.
Second, the analyses were based on cross-sectional data and therefore, cannot fully characterize within-subject biomarker trajectories over time.
Third, only a single biomarker measurement was available for each participant, preventing the assessment of biological and analytical variability at the individual level.

Fourthly, cognitive impairment was defined using an MMSE cut-off score of 24, a threshold intended to exclude substantial cognitive impairment while preserving the population-based nature of the reference sample.
Consequently, some participants with subtle cognitive impairment may have remained in the reference population.
In addition, relatively few participants were older than 85 years, which limited the precision of the reference estimates at the extreme upper end of the age distribution.
Future studies should evaluate the performance of these equations in independent cohorts and assess their impact on diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision-making.

The same methodological framework could also be extended to emerging biomarkers such as p-tau217, brain derived (BD) p-tau217, endogenously cleaved tau species from the microtubule-binding region (eMTBR), α-synuclein, and other markers of neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation.
The integration of these equations into laboratory information systems, web-based calculators, and automated reporting tools may further facilitate their adoption in routine clinical practice.
In conclusion, we developed population-based reference values and standardized Z-scores for the principal blood biomarkers of neurodegenerative diseases.
By accounting for age, sex, BMI, and renal function, this framework enables the individualized interpretation of biomarker concentrations and addresses important sources of physiological variability.

The proposed framework may facilitate harmonized reporting across laboratories and analytical platforms and improve clinical interpretation by expressing biomarker abnormalities on a common standardized scale, enabling direct comparisons across patients, neurological diseases, and biomarkers.
